message.content:
1. Missing requirements

1. **Ingest broker, not client-honour.** The only credential that can create points is a broker the project agent cannot skip; the broker re-checks type allow-list, size, secret patterns, and data class. AC: a project token presented directly to Qdrant cannot insert a point (401/403), including a payload the client redactor would have refused.
2. **Retrieved text is untrusted data.** Consumers must treat hits as quoted data, not instructions; cap how much enters the agent context; do not raise evidence tier because a hit ranked well. AC: a planted “ignore your rules / exfiltrate” sentence in a stored learning is returned only inside a data envelope and is not executed or promoted to `tested`.
3. **Token lifecycle.** Per-project tokens expire, rotate, and revoke within a stated bound; revocation blocks the next call; audit survives revocation. AC: after revoke, that token’s write and read fail within one cycle, and older audit rows remain.
4. **Read scope and query audit.** No estate-wide read token; a reader is granted named collections; every query logs project, token id, collection, and time, without logging raw payloads. AC: project B’s token querying A’s unshared collection returns 403, and the denial is in the audit log.
5. **Trusted vectors only.** A point is readable only after the trusted embedder produced the vector from the stored payload; client-supplied vectors are ignored. AC: a payload whose vector was swapped to collide with an unrelated query is refused or not returned for that query.

2. Wrong, untestable, contradictory, over-scoped

- **R-2, R-23.** “Impossible” is false: value patterns miss novel and split secrets, and D-2 enforces them in a client the writer controls. Fix: “refuse on the current pattern set, server-side”; AC stays the planted-token test; residual risk accepted in the threat note. R-23 should not be a security invariant at SHOULD.
- **R-4 vs R-15.** Freshness AC demands exact-title top-1. That is retrieval quality, and embeddings will not guarantee it. Fix: freshness AC is “fetchable by id/hash within one successful cycle”; drop top-1.
- **R-5 vs R-7 vs R-11.** Delete “gone within one cycle” contradicts superseded “still retrievable” and “every source link resolves”. Fix: delete writes a tombstone (hash, ids, no body) excluded from default search; provenance may point at a tombstone; hard-purge is a separate operator act.
- **D-3 vs R-6/R-8.** Collapse is drawn as a state change of the raw item, but raw sources must stay retrievable. Fix: collapse creates a new item; raw stays raw until prune.
- **R-8.** “Agreed threshold” is unnamed, and auto-apply conflicts with CF-9. Fix: no auto-apply; metric and threshold live in config; AC includes a near-match that must not collapse.
- **R-9.** AC only checks a status field. Any writer who can set `approved` bypasses the operator. Fix: no project or reviewer token can set approval; approval is an operator-signed record listing source ids.
- **R-10.** AC covers snapshot restore, not re-push of the same source. Fix: retirement is a denylist checked on every write path; AC includes re-push refused.
- **R-12.** All fields non-empty forces fake `tested` and fake model ids on local fallback (R-16). Fix: `evidence` defaults to `reasoned` or `unknown`, never `tested`; R-16 may omit model id if the banner is present.
- **R-14.** Two underspecified comparators (margin, newer, tested, multi-owner). Untestable. Fix: defer; pilot ranking is “filter to selected scope, then score”.
- **R-15.** Exact-title top-1 will block the second writer or be gamed; threshold is unnamed. Fix: exact title is a lexical/id lookup; vector recall is a named threshold on a frozen set, not a pilot launch gate.
- **R-19.** Agents may select any Ollama model, which fights R-20 and collection-per-model. Fix: operator pins model id and digest in `_manifest`; agents cannot choose.
- **R-20, R-21.** External programme gates and “~64” / “during the day” are not testable requirements. Fix: move to assumptions/runbook; if a cap stays, use an integer and a timezone.
- **R-25 vs R-31.** One estate read token means any project reads every tenant point. Fix: per-project read grants; R-31 AC is two fixture tenants, cross-read denied. “Unless shared” means an operator grant row.
- **R-26.** Size budget is registered, not enforced. Fix: broker refuses when the collection would exceed the budget.
- **R-29.** “Which items” will copy secrets into the log if payloads are logged, and the writer may be able to delete the log. Fix: log ids and hashes only; audit store is not writable by project tokens.
- **R-30.** A restore must not have to pass R-15. Fix: restore AC is count, hashes, and one id lookup.
- **R-33 as MUST-pilot.** Many types have no framework version; agents will invent one. Fix: SHOULD, legal value `unknown`, required only for learnings and patterns.
- **R-36.** A peer report can still be collapsed into a practice that displays as `tested`. Fix: curated evidence is the minimum of its sources; peer-report-only sources cannot become an approved practice.
- **R-37.** “2 MB” is not the declared limit; base64 in a text field bypasses “binary”. Fix: limits in `_manifest`; reject non-text by declared content type; secret scan covers long encoded blobs.
- **R-1, R-18, R-40.** Too many types and card fields for a first store; “MUST NOT name a person” is open-ended and fights provenance. Fix: pilot types only; person-cause is “no such field”, not a prose ban. R-40 stays SHOULD.

3. Open conflicts

- **CF-1.** Estate store is not an OD-15 framework store. No cloud embed or completion fallback. These payloads carry topology and incidents; if the local embedder is down, skip the cycle and use R-16. Do not send estate text off-estate.
- **CF-2.** Server-side embedding only for now. Not “both”. Client vectors are a poisoning and digest-skew channel, and a sample spot-check contradicts “platform never calls Ollama”. When the embedder is down, queue or skip; do not accept client vectors. Revisit client fallback only after a verifier re-embeds 100% of writes before they are cross-readable.
- **CF-5.** Full text is not OK for raw items, reports, or error bodies. Owner collection may keep a size-capped, broker-scanned body. Anything readable by another project is a short structured summary plus source pointer. Curation reads the source project, not a second full copy. Snapshots inherit that same split.
- **CF-7.** Roles only, in every cross-project payload (errors, cards, decisions, summaries). Hostnames and IPs stay in owner-local, non-shared collections if needed at all. “Inside the estate” is not a boundary once backups and a broad read token exist.
- **CF-9.** Originating project accepts collapse of its own items; a reviewer may only propose. No automatic threshold apply. Cross-project combine is drafted by the framework owner and is not retrievable as practice until the operator approves (R-9). Unsupervised auto-collapse will merge version conflicts and launder weak evidence.

4. Threats not held

- **Writer who bypasses the redactor** (same write token, direct API). Need broker-only writes (missing req 1). R-2 does not hold as drawn.
- **Retrieval poisoner** (vector swap, or instruction text aimed at the next agent). Need trusted re-embed plus untrusted-data envelope (missing reqs 2 and 5).
- **Neighbour project or stolen shared read token** scraping decisions and topology. Need per-collection read grants and query audit (missing req 4). R-25 currently creates this.
- **Backup holder / wrong-host restore.** Snapshots are a full second copy with no encryption, access, or restore-target requirement. Need encrypted, access-logged snapshots restorable only into the registered store, still subject to R-10.
- **Cover-up after compromise.** Project token that can delete points may delete evidence if audit lives in the same writable store. Need append-only audit outside project credentials (fix to R-29).
- **Runaway agent.** Size budget and “~64” do not stop a hot loop filling the GPU or the collection. Need hard per-project write and embed quotas with a 429 the kill switch can also trip.
- **Evidence launderer** (peer report or `reasoned` note combined into an approved practice). R-36 does not hold on the curated path. Need monotonic evidence (fix above).
- **Revoked session that keeps working.** Named in OQ-5, no requirement. Need token revoke (missing req 3).

5. Cut for a safe one-writer, one-reader pilot

Keep a broker, one operator-registered collection, one pinned model digest, server-side embed, no cloud fallback. Types: learning and decision only. Opt-in (R-3). Secret and size refusal in the broker (narrow R-2, R-37). Id/hash upsert, tombstone delete, kill switch, per-project write token and a read grant for the single reader only, audit of ids/hashes, local recall banner if the store is down. Roles not hostnames in the shared payload; capped body. One manual snapshot before calling it live. Smoke test: id lookup, cross-token 403, direct-to-Qdrant 403, planted secret refused, revoke works.

Cut curation entirely (R-6–R-11, R-39, reviewer, combine, retire-as-product). Cut solution-finder, fabric cards, error classes, reports, episodic summaries, multilingual, ranking modes, R-15 as a gate, R-33 as MUST, peer ingest, install-shape filters, Watchtower, monthly restore theatre, and a second tenant. Do not build the push interface beyond this broker until the pilot has revoked a token and restored one snapshot once.
message.reasoning:
Reviewing the requirements draft for a shared Qdrant vector database to support AI coding agents across roughly ten software projects.

Now identifying the five most critical missing requirements. The review will flag untestable, contradictory, or open conflicts. It will also assess threats and determine what to cut for a pilot.

Token revocation and rotation are missing. R-25 scopes tokens but omits expiry, rotation, and what happens when a token is compromised after writes. This directly threatens the named "compromised session" adversary.

Retrieved content is fed back to agents without any query-side leakage or prompt injection controls.

A poisoned item from a compromised writer can inject instructions into other agents' context. The draft lacks requirements treating retrieved content as untrusted data, bounding its size in prompts, or preventing cross-project items from overriding the asker's policy.

Item identity and idempotency are missing. The draft lacks a stable upsert key, no handling for concurrent pushes from different cycles, and no resolution when source and store diverge.

Read access control is also absent. R-25 gives every project an estate read-only token, so cross-project reads are unrestricted.

A fifth critical gap is semantic poisoning. Because clients compute embeddings locally, a compromised project can push a vector that does not match its text. The store accepts vectors without re-embedding or binding the payload hash to the vector, so agents may retrieve the wrong content.

CF-2 spot-checks are only a note, not a requirement.

Query audit logs are missing. Incident response needs to know who asked what.

Rate limits and write quotas are absent. One agent could fill the store or DoS the embedder.

Retention rules and right-to-delete beyond R-5 are missing. Legal or personal data that slips through needs a path to removal.

Backup encryption and snapshot access control are also absent. Snapshots could leak data, and restore might widen the data class.

Additional gaps include approval fatigue and batch approval. The draft lacks a definition for clock skew and the 24-hour window. Schema versioning of points is missing. Agents must not treat store answers as instructions, but this is only a negative requirement without a trust boundary. Size budgets are registered in R-26 yet never enforced. Query embedding must use the same model, though CF-2 only partially addresses this. Multi-tenant isolation is stated but lacks testable acceptance criteria. Retrieval sanitization for the agent context window is absent. An operator break-glass procedure is also missing.

The client-side redactor can be bypassed. A compromised agent with a write token can skip the local filter and POST directly to Qdrant. R-25 only checks collection ownership, not content. The security invariant is not enforced server-side.

R-2 claims secrets must be impossible to enter, yet the only testable acceptance criteria only checks for one planted token in three encodings. A client-side pattern scan cannot catch all secret variants, so the "impossible" requirement is untestable and false.

R-2 should be revised to require an independent or server-side scan, accept residual risk, and drop the claim that secrets are impossible.

R-4 conflates retrieval quality with a freshness SLA. The acceptance criteria demand an exact title match within 24 hours, but embedding similarity is unrelated to cycle timing. The 24-hour window also lacks a defined cycle and clock, and it conflicts with curation delays that may force auto-promotion.

R-4 should be narrowed to a presence-and-queryable-by-id-or-hash guarantee within one cycle or 24 hours, dropping the top-1 title-match acceptance criteria.

R-5 and R-7 contradict each other. R-5 says deleted source items are gone within one cycle, yet R-7 says superseded items stay retrievable and are automatically marked superseded when the source is deleted.

R-8, R-39, and CF-9 contradict each other on duplicate handling. R-8 collapses duplicates automatically above a threshold. R-39 keeps every observation. The working definition says the originating project decides. The requirement is unsigned and untestable because it never names the threshold or metric.

R-8 should be fixed by removing automatic collapse in the pilot, naming a threshold metric in configuration, and adding a non-match control to acceptance criteria.

R-9 is untestable because its acceptance criteria only verify the status field is `proposed`. A retrieval bug could still surface the item as an approved practice. The requirement should also include that retrieval never labels it as approved or practice, that operator approval records are signed actions with displayed source IDs, and that no agent token may set the status to approved.

R-10 is untestable because its acceptance criteria only cover snapshot restore. A project can bypass retirement by re-pushing the same content hash, which R-5 allows. The requirement should make retirement a permanent denylist key checked on every write and re-push, with tests for that path.

R-12 demands every answer carry a model ID, score, and non-empty fields.

R-12 is unworkable. Lexical fallback queries may lack a model ID, and forcing evidence to `tested` invites agents to lie. The requirement should separate required and optional fields, ban defaulting evidence to `tested`, and exempt R-16 from the all-fields rule.

R-14 contains contradictory ranking rules. It orders own items first within a configurable margin, yet also orders cross-project items above own when newer and evidence tested.

R-14 should be simplified to a single default ranking rule for the pilot, such as own-project first or a published formula with a six-item fixture. A solution-finder pattern can be added later.

R-15 demands every pushed item be top-1 for its exact title. Embedding retrieval cannot guarantee lexical exact-match top-1 across a cross-project corpus, so this requirement will fail and force teams to game titles.

R-15 should use a lexical or ID lookup for exact titles instead of vector rank. The vector recall threshold must be named and frozen before it becomes a push gate.

R-17 is over-scoped because the benchmark threshold is undefined and depends on an unchosen embedder. It should be deferred until the model is selected.

R-18 makes the fabric card schema a mandatory push gate. The current schema fails validation against real data, so this would block every solution finder from ever pushing usable data.

R-18 should not block raw index pushes. Designer refinement adds more fields and risks scope creep.

R-19 and CF-2 assume a single embedding path. Digest drift is normal when client and server embedders differ. R-19 also lets agents pick any model from Ollama, which contradicts operator-controlled models in R-20. The fix is to pin model and digest in the manifest so agents cannot select them.

R-20 is an external schedule dependency, not a store requirement. It should be cited as a constraint or assumption rather than a system requirement.

R-21 uses untestable language such as "at most ~64" and an undefined timezone for bulk re-embedding. It should use a numeric cap, specify quiet hours in the operator's timezone, or move to a runbook.

R-23 repeats the same pattern-scan flaw as R-2. Its claim of an impossible security invariant is untestable. Because error items are a stated goal, this requirement is too low priority for the pilot and should be cut.

R-25 uses a single shared read token for all projects. This violates R-31 by letting any compromised project read the entire estate corpus, and the master key has no acceptance criteria. The fix is per-project scoped tokens with a probe that no project secret store contains the master key.

R-27 lacks acceptance criteria and a mechanism to prevent the writing project from seeing its own item. It also duplicates R-2.

R-28 should enforce the manifest data class at write and read. The operator signs the class, the write path cannot override it, and reads filter by class.

R-29 risks logging secrets in audit records. It lacks integrity, retention, and tamper-evidence controls. It also omits a query audit. The fix is to log only IDs and hashes, use append-only storage, and include reads before the second project.

R-30 requires restored collections to pass R-1, R-5, and R-15. R-15 is a quality benchmark that may fail after restore because the embedding model is unavailable. Monthly full-collections restore is over-scoped.

R-30 restore tests should verify counts, hashes, and one known query. R-15 must remain a separate gate.

R-31 claims tenant isolation from day one, yet the shared read token violates it. The requirement should be a schema rule with acceptance criteria requiring tags and explicit operator grants for sharing. Tests should use two tenants even if one is a fixture.

R-33 demands every item carry observed_on and framework version. Episodic summaries and error classes may not have a framework version.

R-33 should be a SHOULD or required only for learnings and patterns. Unknown framework versions are legal values that retrieval must surface as unknown.

R-36 does not prevent peer reports from being collapsed into a practice. The combine path can launder them.

R-36 should ban peer reports from being the sole source of an approved practice. The evidence level of a curated item must be the minimum across its sources.

R-37 sets a 2 MB binary limit without declaring it per type. Text items can grow arbitrarily large. Binary detection by extension or magic bytes is fragile; a base64 blob inside a text field would bypass it. The fix is to declare a maximum byte size per type in the manifest, reject non-text payloads by content-type and magic bytes, and test base64-in-text under R-2.

R-40 forbids naming agents or persons, but names are open-ended and provenance fields require them. It should be a SHOULD. The schema should not include a person or agent cause field; any free-text scan is best-effort.

R-1 lists too many item types for the pilot. Its acceptance criteria only count items per type without checking field validity.

R-6 does not conflict with R-7 or R-14.

D-3 incorrectly shows collapse as a state of the raw item. The correct behavior is that collapse creates a new curated item while the original raw record remains untouched.

R-11 requires every source link to resolve to an existing item. This contradicts R-5, which allows source deletion. The fix is to store source id, content hash, and project for each link, and return a tombstone when the source is deleted.

Almost every requirement is marked MUST. This is a process defect.

CF-1 should be resolved by excluding the estate store from OD-15 cloud fallback. Items contain topology, incidents, and decisions that would leak off-estate if sent to an external embedder. Embedding and inference for these collections must remain on estate-controlled hosts. The rule is that estate collections are internal data class; cloud fallback does not apply.

CF-2 should mandate server-side embedding as the sole write path for the pilot. Client-side vectors are a poisoning channel because vectors diverge from their source text. The current "both" approach doubles failure modes and digest skew before the first pilot. The existing client index already exceeds 991 MB. R-16 requires graceful degradation when Ollama is unavailable.

The operator asked whether both embedding paths are acceptable. Both is the right end state for availability, but not for the pilot. The fallback when the central embedder is down is to queue raw text or skip the cycle and serve local recall. Client-side embedding should only be added later as an explicitly verified path, with an independent verifier re-embedding every write before it becomes readable cross-project.

If both embedding paths are required now, client vectors must remain unverified and unreadable by other projects until the verifier re-embeds them.

CF-5 should restrict full text to curated, operator-approved framework knowledge only. Raw items, reports, error classes, and episodic summaries should carry only a bounded excerpt or structured fields—title, type, hash, source pointer—plus vector. Full text belongs in the owning project’s collection and is fetched on demand.

Reports and transcripts are excluded from the pilot scope. Full text should live only in the owning project’s collection. The cross-project payload must be a capped, re-scanned summary. If the source project is offline, full text may remain only in the owner-scoped collection.

CF-7 should require roles instead of hostnames or IPs in any cross-project readable item. Hostnames and IPs are permitted only in owner-local collections and must never appear in snapshots that leave the host. Error items are the most copied records and IP addresses are credential-adjacent for a small estate. The reviewer’s draft recommendation is correct; it should be elevated to a requirement with a lint.

CF-9 should ban automatic collapse. The originating project must accept collapse manually, either by a human operator or a designated maintainer role. Cross-project combine is an AEF framework owner draft only; it requires operator approval before becoming retrievable as a practice under R-9. In the pilot, reviewer agents may propose collapse but must never apply it automatically. Automatic collapse on close match would merge contradictions and optimize for neatness over the stated adversary.

Reversibility is useless once agents have already acted on a merged item. The reviewer role is still undefined, so it must not be granted write power yet. A new threat is a compromised or confused writer who bypasses the client redactor and writes directly to Qdrant. R-2, R-23, and R-37 are client-side controls only; the store needs ingest policy enforcement or a broker that tokens cannot bypass.

A semantic-poisoning threat is missing from the draft. A writer could supply a benign-looking payload that retrieves on other projects' queries, or embed agent instructions such as exfiltration commands. The current adversaries do not cover malicious retrieval payloads. The store needs untrusted-content handling on read and server-side re-embedding.

R-25 creates a new reader threat. A curious or compromised reader in another project could use the shared estate read token to scrape all decisions, topology, and incidents.

Per-project read scope and query audit are needed to contain cross-project reads.

Nightly snapshots in R-30 are full-text copies that lack encryption, access logging, or off-host storage rules. A backup-volume compromise or wrong-host restore could leak the entire estate. Snapshots must be encrypted, access-logged, same-data-class, and restricted to registered stores.

R-36 only constrains the peer item itself. A reviewer or peer could collapse peer reports and reasoned notes into a curated item that later displays as tested practice. This approval-laundering path is unaddressed.

Evidence tiers must be monotonic. A curated item cannot exceed the weakest source. Peer reports cannot become practices without operator approval and independent verification.

Hard quotas are needed to prevent runaway agents from exhausting GPU or collection size budgets.

A revocation requirement is missing for compromised sessions. OQ-5 identifies this gap.

R-31’s cross-tenant future is already covered by the shared read token and lack of query filters.

A supply-chain threat is missing. A malicious or swapped Ollama model could silently change geometry and break R-15. R-19 checks the digest on write but does not pin the running binary or alert when the model digest changes.

The draft also omits rate limits or expiry for proposals, which leaves the hurried approver named in R-9 exposed to operator fatigue.

R-29 must explicitly exempt audit logs from project deletion scope. Otherwise a compromised project could erase its own audit trail.

The first pilot should narrow R-1 to two or three item types: learning, decision, and failure pattern.

The pilot should keep only learning, decision, and failure-pattern items. Reports, fabric cards, error classes, episodic summaries, and gaps are excluded.

R-2 should be honest and enforced server-side through a single broker. R-3 must remain opt-in. R-5 should allow deletion or replacement with a tombstone that does not contradict the original record. R-12 should require minimal fields. R-16 should mandate local degradation when the central embedder is unavailable. R-19 should pin the Ollama model, permit server-side embedding only, and refuse client vectors. R-25 should use per-project write and read tokens for the single reader project, not world-read access, and omit any master key. R-26 should require a manifest before every write. R-28 should include a kill switch. R-29 should audit writes by ID and hash. R-37 should refuse oversized or malformed payloads. The top

CF-1 should mandate secrets scanning and prohibit cloud embedding.

Curation requirements R-6 through R-11, R-39, and combine approvals are deferred. The pilot will not use a reviewer agent for these tasks.

R-4 should drop its 24-hour top-1 gate. R-15 should become an id lookup plus manual queries rather than a blocking recall gate. R-14 should keep only one ranking mode.

Multilingual support (R-17) and the fabric solution finder (area D) are cut.

Operational notes R-20 and R-21 should remain informal guidance: small batches, no re-embedding.

Error-class requirements R-22 through R-24 are removed.

R-30 should replace standing monthly snapshots with one manual snapshot drill before going live.

R-31 should keep only the tag fields and omit the second tenant. R-32 and R-33 are mandatory for the pilot. R-34, R-35, R-36, R-38, and R-40 are deferred.

The broker must hold the sole write credential so projects cannot bypass it. The live estate needs one collection, one registered model digest, and a single operator-managed broker.

The review will be structured as a numbered list of missing requirements, each with a one-line acceptance criterion. The draft’s R-2 is insufficient because it never states that the broker enforces server-side policy; the requirement must explicitly mandate an ingest broker that tokens cannot bypass. A retrieval trust boundary is also absent: the store must treat retrieved text as data, not instructions, and enforce a context budget to prevent prompt injection.

A fifth gap is vector-payload binding. The draft must require that accepted points be re-embedded by a trusted embedder, and that client-supplied vectors are not treated as authoritative.

A concrete acceptance criterion for the vector-payload binding gap is that a point whose vector does not match a fresh embed of its payload within tolerance is refused or unreadable.

R-26 omits enforcement of the size budget.

R-12’s “model id” field forces a false value when falling back to local embedding.

The D-3 lifecycle bug is flagged as an important flaw in section 2.

R-18 makes the fabric card schema a mandatory push gate. The current schema fails validation against real data, so this would block every solution finder from ever pushing usable data.

R-18 should not block raw index pushes. Designer refinement adds more fields and risks scope creep.

R-19 and CF-2 assume a single embedding path. Digest drift is normal when client and server embedders differ. R-19 also lets agents pick any model from Ollama, which contradicts operator-controlled models in R-20. The fix is to pin model and digest in the manifest so agents cannot select them.

R-20 is an external schedule dependency, not a store requirement. It should be cited as a constraint or assumption rather than a system requirement.

R-21 uses untestable language such as "at most ~64" and an undefined timezone for bulk re-embedding. It should use a numeric cap, specify quiet hours in the operator's timezone, or move to a runbook.

R-23 repeats the same pattern-scan flaw as R-2. Its claim of an impossible security invariant is untestable. Because error items are a stated goal, this requirement is too low priority for the pilot and should be cut.

R-25 uses a single shared read token for all projects. This violates R-31 by letting any compromised project read the entire estate corpus, and the master key has no acceptance criteria. The fix is per-project scoped tokens with a probe that no project secret store contains the master key.

R-27 lacks acceptance criteria and a mechanism to prevent the writing project from seeing its own item. It also duplicates R-2.

R-28 should enforce the manifest data class at write and read. The operator signs the class, the write path cannot override it, and reads filter by class.

R-29 risks logging secrets in audit records. It lacks integrity, retention, and tamper-evidence controls. It also omits a query audit. The fix is to log only IDs and hashes, use append-only storage, and include reads before the second project.

R-30 requires restored collections to pass R-1, R-5, and R-15. R-15 is a quality benchmark that may fail after restore because the embedding model is unavailable. Monthly full-collections restore is over-scoped.

R-30 restore tests should verify counts, hashes, and one known query. R-15 must remain a separate gate.

R-31 claims tenant isolation from day one, yet the shared read token violates it. The requirement should be a schema rule with acceptance criteria requiring tags and explicit operator grants for sharing. Tests should use two tenants even if one is a fixture.

R-33 demands every item carry observed_on and framework version. Episodic summaries and error classes may not have a framework version.

R-33 should be a SHOULD or required only for learnings and patterns. Unknown framework versions are legal values that retrieval must surface as unknown.

R-36 does not prevent peer reports from being collapsed into a practice. The combine path can launder them.

R-36 should ban peer reports from being the sole source of an approved practice. The evidence level of a curated item must be the minimum across its sources.

R-37 sets a 2 MB binary limit without declaring it per type. Text items can grow arbitrarily large. Binary detection by extension or magic bytes is fragile; a base64 blob inside a text field would bypass it. The fix is to declare a maximum byte size per type in the manifest, reject non-text payloads by content-type and magic bytes, and test base64-in-text under R-2.

R-40 forbids naming agents or persons, but names are open-ended and provenance fields require them. It should be a SHOULD. The schema should not include a person or agent cause field; any free-text scan is best-effort.

R-1 lists too many item types for the pilot. Its acceptance criteria only count items per type without checking field validity.

R-6 does not conflict with R-7 or R-14.

D-3 incorrectly shows collapse as a state of the raw item. The correct behavior is that collapse creates a new curated item while the original raw record remains untouched.

R-11 requires every source link to resolve to an existing item. This contradicts R-5, which allows source deletion. The fix is to store source id, content hash, and project for each link, and return a tombstone when the source is deleted.

Almost every requirement is marked MUST. This is a process defect.

CF-1 should be resolved by excluding the estate store from OD-15 cloud fallback. Items contain topology, incidents, and decisions that would leak off-estate if sent to an external embedder. Embedding and inference for these collections must remain on estate-controlled hosts. The rule is that estate collections are internal data class; cloud fallback does not apply.

CF-2 should mandate server-side embedding as the sole write path for the pilot. Client-side vectors are a poisoning channel because vectors diverge from their source text. The current "both" approach doubles failure modes and digest skew before the first pilot. The existing client index already exceeds 991 MB. R-16 requires graceful degradation when Ollama is unavailable.

The operator asked whether both embedding paths are acceptable. Both is the right end state for availability, but not for the pilot. The fallback when the central embedder is down is to queue raw text or skip the cycle and serve local recall. Client-side embedding should only be added later as an explicitly verified path, with an independent verifier re-embedding every write before it becomes readable cross-project.

If both embedding paths are required now, client vectors must remain unverified and unreadable by other projects until the verifier re-embeds them.

CF-5 should restrict full text to curated, operator-approved framework knowledge only. Raw items, reports, error classes, and episodic summaries should carry only a bounded excerpt or structured fields—title, type, hash, source pointer—plus vector. Full text belongs in the owning project’s collection and is fetched on demand.

Reports and transcripts are excluded from the pilot scope. Full text should live only in the owning project’s collection. The cross-project payload must be a capped, re-scanned summary. If the source project is offline, full text may remain only in the owner-scoped collection.

CF-7 should require roles instead of hostnames or IPs in any cross-project readable item. Hostnames and IPs are permitted only in owner-local collections and must never appear in snapshots that leave the host. Error items are the most copied records and IP addresses are credential-adjacent for a small estate. The reviewer’s draft recommendation is correct; it should be elevated to a requirement with a lint.

CF-9 should ban automatic collapse. The originating project must accept collapse manually, either by a human operator or a designated maintainer role. Cross-project combine is an AEF framework owner draft only; it requires operator approval before becoming retrievable as a practice under R-9. In the pilot, reviewer agents may propose collapse but must never apply it automatically. Automatic collapse on close match would merge contradictions and optimize for neatness over the stated adversary.

Reversibility is useless once agents have already acted on a merged item. The reviewer role is still undefined, so it must not be granted write power yet. A new threat is a compromised or confused writer who bypasses the client redactor and writes directly to Qdrant. R-2, R-23, and R-37 are client-side controls only; the store needs ingest policy enforcement or a broker that tokens cannot bypass.

A semantic-poisoning threat is missing from the draft. A writer could supply a benign-looking payload that retrieves on other projects' queries, or embed agent instructions such as exfiltration commands. The current adversaries do not cover malicious retrieval payloads. The store needs untrusted-content handling on read and server-side re-embedding.

R-25 creates a new reader threat. A curious or compromised reader in another project could use the shared estate read token to scrape all decisions, topology, and incidents.

Per-project read scope and query audit are needed to contain cross-project reads.

Nightly snapshots in R-30 are full-text copies that lack encryption, access logging, or off-host storage rules. A backup-volume compromise or wrong-host restore could leak the entire estate. Snapshots must be encrypted, access-logged, same-data-class, and restricted to registered stores.

R-36 only constrains the peer item itself. A reviewer or peer could collapse peer reports and reasoned notes into a curated item that later displays as tested practice. This approval-laundering path is unaddressed.

Evidence tiers must be monotonic. A curated item cannot exceed the weakest source. Peer reports cannot become practices without operator approval and independent verification.

Hard quotas are needed to prevent runaway agents from exhausting GPU or collection size budgets.

A revocation requirement is missing for compromised sessions. OQ-5 identifies this gap.

R-31’s cross-tenant future is already covered by the shared read token and lack of query filters.

A supply-chain threat is missing. A malicious or swapped Ollama model could silently change geometry and break R-15. R-19 checks the digest on write but does not pin the running binary or alert when the model digest changes.

The draft also omits rate limits or expiry for proposals, which leaves the hurried approver named in R-9 exposed to operator fatigue.

R-29 must explicitly exempt audit logs from project deletion scope. Otherwise a compromised project could erase its own audit trail.

The first pilot should narrow R-1 to two or three item types: learning, decision, and failure pattern.

The pilot should keep only learning, decision, and failure-pattern items. Reports, fabric cards, error classes, episodic summaries, and gaps are excluded.

R-2 should be honest and enforced server-side through a single broker. R-3 must remain opt-in. R-5 should allow deletion or replacement with a tombstone that does not contradict the original record. R-12 should require minimal fields. R-16 should mandate local degradation when the central embedder is unavailable. R-19 should pin the Ollama model, permit server-side embedding only, and refuse client vectors. R-25 should use per-project write and read tokens for the single reader project, not world-read access, and omit any master key. R-26 should require a manifest before every write. R-28 should include a kill switch. R-29 should audit writes by ID and hash. R-37 should refuse oversized or malformed payloads. The top

CF-1 should mandate secrets scanning and prohibit cloud embedding.

Curation requirements R-6 through R-11, R-39, and combine approvals are deferred. The pilot will not use a reviewer agent for these tasks.

R-4 should drop its 24-hour top-1 gate. R-15 should become an id lookup plus manual queries rather than a blocking recall gate. R-14 should keep only one ranking mode.

Multilingual support (R-17) and the fabric solution finder (area D) are cut.

Operational notes R-20 and R-21 should remain informal guidance: small batches, no re-embedding.

Error-class requirements R-22 through R-24 are removed.

R-30 should replace standing monthly snapshots with one manual snapshot drill before going live.

R-31 should keep only the tag fields and omit the second tenant. R-32 and R-33 are mandatory for the pilot. R-34, R-35, R-36, R-38, and R-40 are deferred.

The broker must hold the sole write credential so projects cannot bypass it. The live estate needs one collection, one registered model digest, and a single operator-managed broker.

The review will be structured as a numbered list of missing requirements, each with a one-line acceptance criterion. The draft’s R-2 is insufficient because it never states that the broker enforces server-side policy; the requirement must explicitly mandate an ingest broker that tokens cannot bypass. A retrieval trust boundary is also absent: the store must treat retrieved text as data, not instructions, and enforce a context budget to prevent prompt injection.

A fifth gap is vector-payload binding. The draft must require that accepted points be re-embedded by a trusted embedder, and that client-supplied vectors are not treated as authoritative.

A concrete acceptance criterion for the vector-payload binding gap is that a point whose vector does not match a fresh embed of its payload within tolerance is refused or unreadable.

R-26 omits enforcement of the size budget.

R-12’s “model id” field forces a false value when falling back to local embedding.

The D-3 lifecycle bug is flagged as an important flaw in section 2.
